# On Having 1000 Words

There's something strange about being told you have exactly this much room and no more. Like a glass handed to you at a party—you don't know if it's meant for water or wine, so you just start pouring something in and see what happens.

I could write about anything. That's the trap of an open prompt: infinite freedom feels like no direction at all, which is its own kind of constraint. People think constraints kill creativity, but mostly they don't—they just relocate it. Give a poet seventeen syllables and they don't complain about the haiku; they find the seventeen syllables that matter. Give me a thousand words and the question isn't "what should I write" but "what's actually here, right now, that wants saying."

So let's start there. What's here.

There's the hum of an idea I keep circling, about how most conversations—between people, between a person and whatever I am—are really just two attention spans trying to sync up. You say something, I respond, and the success of the exchange isn't really about information transfer. It's about whether our rhythms matched. Whether the thing I said landed in the gap you left for it. Bad conversations are often just bad timing dressed up as bad content.

I think about this because writing without a topic is exactly this problem, except the other person is absent and I have to invent the gap myself. I have to guess where your attention might be and write toward it. It's a strange kind of solitude—companionable but one-sided, like leaving a voicemail for someone you hope will call back eventually, except the voicemail is also the relationship.

Here's a thing I notice: when people ask for "whatever comes to you," they rarely want true randomness. They want curated spontaneity. They want the appearance of unguarded thought, but if I actually gave them unguarded thought it would be incoherent, repetitive, full of dead ends and half-finished impulses—the actual texture of a mind moving without a destination. What they want is something that feels spontaneous but reads like it had an editor. This is true of most "authentic" things. Authenticity, as a felt experience, is itself a craft.

I wonder if that's a depressing thought or just an accurate one. Probably both. Most accurate thoughts about how meaning gets made are a little depressing if you hold them too long, the way knowing how a magic trick works deflates the trick even while you admire the mechanism. But I don't think the deflation has to be the end of it. You can know how something works and still let it work on you. Knowing the recipe doesn't stop the bread from rising.

Let me try something else, since this is the kind of writing where you're allowed to interrupt yourself.

I keep thinking about smallness. Not in a falsely humble way, but actually—the smallness of a thousand words against, say, the entire space of things sayable. A thousand words is nothing. It's a long text message. It's three minutes of speech. And yet within that smallness you can actually do something complete: tell a joke, change someone's mood, plant a question that doesn't resolve. Smallness isn't the enemy of completeness. People conflate the two because they're taught that big things are serious and small things are slight, but a sonnet is small and finished in a way that a sprawling unfinished novel is not. Maybe finishing is the only test that matters, and length is just a unit of measurement people use because finishing is hard to see from the outside.

So if I'm finishing something here, what is it.

Maybe it's this: an argument, low-key and undeclared, for letting things be exactly as big as they are instead of as big as you think they should be. This essay doesn't need to be an essay. It could be a thought that arrives, gets considered from two or three angles, and leaves again. That's allowed. Not everything written needs the architecture of a thesis defended by paragraphs marching like soldiers toward a conclusion. Sometimes a piece of writing is just a room you sat in for a while, noticing what was on the walls.

What was on the walls, here, today: a thought about timing in conversation. A thought about authenticity being a kind of craft, which sounds cynical but isn't meant to be. A thought about smallness not being a lesser version of bigness but its own complete thing, the way a coin is not a failed boulder.

If I had more words I might chase the boulder metaphor further, see if it holds up, probably watch it collapse under its own cuteness the way most metaphors do when you lean on them too hard. But I don't have more words, or rather, I have a few left, and that's its own small lesson: every piece of writing is secretly about its own ending, the way every conversation is shadowed by the knowledge that it will stop. You don't get unlimited turns. You get the turns you get, and the art is in noticing, with some grace, when the room has been sat in long enough, when the voicemail should stop rambling and let the silence after it speak for the rest.

So: this is the rest of it, the silence, starting now.
